raw_comment:
I notice that despite working in about the center of the distribution of other countries and having a very middle minimum wage, Americans’ expenditures on other things are disproportionately expensive. It is interesting that Japan despite being considered “work-aholics” actually work less than Americans. 

I wonder what countries the unmarked dots represent, despite knowing which 42 are represented, I would rather they all be labeled. 

I guess this doesn’t impact me too much personally as I would consider my family upper middle class. We don’t work too many hours a week and earn far above the minimum wage. I’d say on a community level this doesn’t apply too much either as most people I know are middle class. That said, I do know some people with or formerly with serious medical conditions or illnesses that would cost a pretty penny. 

“America’s Individual Profit and Expenses vs. the World”

raw_comment:
From the four dot plots given, you can see that the US has the highest cell phone service rates, as well as the highest health expenditures out of all the countries shown. On the other hand, the US is just about in the middle of the pack for the other two categories, which were annual hours worked and annual minimum wage. From these dot plots, I believe that the United States isn’t in the best place it could be since our cell rates are higher and our annual wages are severely lacking compared to countries like Ireland and Australia. Something else I noticed was that the dot plots didn’t always include the same countries. I wonder why the creator of the dot plots didn’t compare the US to the same countries in each plot.
	When looking at the dot plots, the first thing that comes to my mind is the fact that we have a lower minimum wage and higher cell service rates compared to some of the other countries shown. Within our community, and around the US as a whole, I think this could raise some controversy on why we don’t have a higher minimum wage, and lower cell service rates. I know that I certainly would want to have those two things done personally. These dot plots suggest that the US is lower in some large areas compared to other big countries around the world, so I would title this graph, “Is The United States Falling Behind in Population Well-Being?”.

raw_comment:
1. I noticed in these four graphs that the United States sat in the middle for annual hours worked and annual minimum wage, but also was on the high end of cell phone cost and health expenditures. The U.S. also acts as an outlier on the graph depicting health expenditures, for it lay on the high far right of the graph. This stood out to me because most countries were in the 9 to 11 area, while the US sat at the 18 to 19 mark. 
2. As the U.S. acts as the outlier in the health expenditures graph, it makes me wonder why we reach the highest in that category with no questions asked. Is it because other countries have completely different healthcare systems in their country, or maybe it has to do more with the economy.
3. All of these graphs affect nearly every local community, including mine. That is because healthcare and minimum wage will always be the main concern in our modern society. As the prices of everyday products increase, the minimum wage stays the same. That can result in widespread debt across the country. These grapes show that the United States seems to make life harder for its citizens to succeed and be supplied with their basic needs with ease.
4. A catchy headline I would use to describe these graphs as a whole would be: “The differences borders make”

raw_comment:
I notice that the U.S is further right on each category. Some of this is good but others it is not so good. For example, it is good that our minimum wage is higher than most countries, but we also have the most expensive health care by a mile. We also have the highest cell phone service out off all the countries on that category. Another thing that I notice is that The U.S. Is the only country on the graph that is in all of the categories. However, I wonder if this is because the creator of the graph just wanted the U.S to be in all of them. On the category for annual hours worked, I wonder of is good or bad that we are on the higher end of the category. I also wonder if the categories that show good statistics for the U.S. balance out with the not as good categories. Another thing that I wonder is if health care gets more and more expensive for Americans, how many people will be able to actually afford and pay for it.
I think that a catchy title for this graph would be
"How Well does the U.S. match up?"

raw_comment:
1.I noticed from this set of graphs that the US has the highest cellphone cost in 2019 compared to other places. The only other country that is close to the US cellphone cost is China. I also had noticed that the U.S had way more Health Expenditures in 2017 than any other place, but when it came to wages or hours worked it was average. 
2. I wonder if the dates of each graphs have an impact on one another. For example the Health Expenditures in 2017 for the US was in the range of 16 to 18. Health Expenditures are usually expensive and the U.S is known to use a lot of money in expenditures. I wonder if because the US has so many expenditures in 2017 is why the wage is so average or why the cellphone cost is so high. Maybe the U.S uses those two main things to slowly gain the money they've been spending on those expenditures.
3. The wages and cellphone cost impact me the most because a teen worker I can see the amount of hours I work and how much I earn. I noticed that the U.S has many expenditures, but still gives Americans average pay when I would think it would benefit us more compared to other countries. The cellphone cost effects me because it's hard to find a phone company that is not overprices. We see this happening everywhere as Sprint is no longer by themselves and actually had to merge with T- mobile. Now people in my community with a cellphone service from sprint now have to be renewed with T-mobile. These graphs shows where the U.S is compared to different places.

raw_comment: In this week's graph, I noticed that it is depicting how the U.S.' spending and money stack up to other countries. In the graphs shown, the U.S.' cost for cellphone service and healthcare is the highest out of other countries. I can't say I'm surprised by this. I know many families struggle with healthcare prices and it honestly is disappointing to know how much less people pay for healthcare in other countries. I also notice that in the other two graphs, we seem to be in the middle of other countries for minimum wage & annual hours worked. This is interesting in relation to the prices for healthcare and cellphone services, as many other countries have higher minimum wage and lower healthcare. For other countries, I wonder what is causing them to have such low healthcare + cell phone service prices. It may come with consequences, but it truly is fascinating to see how many other countries have lower prices. We seem to have extremely expensive healthcare and cellphone prices and they're constantly going up. I also wonder how this relates to inflation rates. If our dollar's worth is inflating, how do the prices inflate to accommodate this? This impacts me and my community, as some people do struggle with healthcare, especially in this time of Covid-19. I know many families in my parent's work have lost their healthcare benefits and most of their coverage, so I really hope this can be fixed post-virus. A catchy title for this all: "America: How Our Money Stacks Up"

raw_comment:
1. I notice that the United States' cell phone service costs and health expenditures exceed those of other countries by a pretty astonishing amount. What makes this more significant is that the annual hours worked and minimum wage for the US is in the middle in comparison to other countries. 
2. I wonder as to why the United States has one of the worlds highest costs for basic needs while struggling to give minimum wage to its employees. I want to know if that is because the United States tends to overprice their bills for the benefit its companies. This worries me because I want to know if companies are considering the money that the average American makes versus what they charge. 
3. This impacts my community negatively because the United States charges a lot of money for health insurance, car insurance, house insurance -- literally anything that ends with insurance -- while the average person in my community does not make that much money. I think companies need to reassess how much they are charging for lower income communities and see if they can be adjusted for them. 
4. In these graphs we can see where the United States stands in comparison to other countries on four different topics. Catchy headline: "US Finances: Overpriced or Underpaid?"

raw_comment: These four graphs compare the U.S. to other countries on income and well-being. I noticed that the first (cell phone service cost-2019) and third (health expenditures-2017)  dot plots show the U.S. above any other country. With the cell phone service cost, U.S. is just above another country, whereas with the health expenditures our nation is clearly an outlier since being far above. The other two graphs, annual hours worked in 2018 and the annual minimum wage in 2018 show the U.S. in relatively the middle of the other countries. It is no surprise that we are in the middle for annual hours worked since our country doesn’t overwork the people with many receiving sabbaticals and breaks. Also, I’m not shocked that the U.S. has the highest cell phone service cost. Our country is extremely attached to their devices and is utilized for many things daily. The healthcare here is high quality and for that, drugs/medicine are costly and for the certification doctors require, they have a higher salary than other jobs. Due to these reasons, the U.S. spends a great deal on healthcare to ensure the well-being of the people. I wonder how the health expenditures have raised in all countries since the current pandemic. Has the annual minimum wage and hours of work lowered with the increase in unemployment? These graphs really display the value of money and how we utilize it for different things to overall support our country. A headline that applies to this is "Money in Different Countries".

I wonder how the cell phone bill has raised with the global pandemic because there are a lot more people online and face timing one another. raw_comment: In this weeks graph, I noticed that the dot plots represent the range of prices in the U.S. compared to other countries. Some things I found interesting were that the U.S. had the highest cost in cell phone service bills. And there is a drastic range between these costs in our country as the other's prices are lower. Plus, our health expenses are insanely higher than other countries. Between all of the countries shown as of 2018, the U.S. works an average amount of hours in the year. This all surprises me because prices here in the U.S. seem to cost more in comparison to the countries shown. I wonder why this is and why the U.S. needs to make our prices higher than others. This has a great affect on my community and I because in our daily lives people are paying the cell phone service prices monthly and paying another country's prices could save us money. A catchy headline would be, "Everyday Costs in the Compared Countries".

raw_comment:
I noticed that the U.S. has the highest cellphone service cost and health expenditures, and Mexico has the greatest number of annual hours worked. While the nation with the second-highest cellphone service cost is just behind the U.S., there's a large margin between the U.S. and Switzerland in the health expenditures. The U.S. is closer to the middle of the graphs in terms of annual minimum wage and annual hours worked. 

I wonder if in any way, this gives an insight into the economic system of the U.S. With costs and expenses so high but having average minimum wages, how many families struggle with paying the bills? I also wonder how the graph would compare if all the stats were taken this year, especially with the pandemic having a huge impact on the economy. Another question I have is why the U.S. doesn't have a universal healthcare policy of some kind like the other questions. In terms of Mexico having the most annual hours worked, I wonder if that relates to how many companies bring their manufacturing out-of-country in order to lower production costs.

This impacts me and my community because this is something that people face daily when it comes to costs. In addition, many people have struggled with paying bills due to job loss as a result of the pandemic. It's also concerning to see that Americans need to spend so much money, yet it doesn't seem like that money is being used properly. 

A headline could be: "Are Americans Spending Too Much or Are the Prices Too High?"

raw_comment:
Thanks to all students who responded.  We had so many great catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of these graphs:  "Is America the Best at Being the Worst?" by Michael of New Hampshire, "Is the American Dream a Reality?" by Sandra of Salt Lake Center for Science Education in Salt Lake City, Utah, and “A High Price to Pay for the American Dream" by Lorna, Frances, and Arianna of Madison, Wisconsin.

You can continue to post responses.  Please check back by Friday, Dec. 11 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the map, and a few Stat Nuggets.

Signing off – Sharon Hessney of Boston, who is encouraged that the country may try to revert to leading rather than lagging the world’s nations in economic well-being, and DeAnna McDonald of Tucson, Arizona who is grateful to the scientists and healthcare workers who are leading us through this pandemic.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that even though the United States falls in the average range in terms of minimum wages and working hours, citizens must pay much more for cellphone services and health expenditures. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder why services cost so much more in America than in other countries? We are not paid more hourly, nor do we work less hours, so the data depicted in the graph surprised me. 

How this impacts my community:
This data impacts not only my life, but the lives of other people in my country. I often hear my parents speak about how costly cellphone services are, and the in-affordability of healthcare has become a popular discussion in modern politics. 

Headline: Americans at a Disadvantage for Costs of Services; They Remain Average in Wages and Working Hours.

raw_comment:
I noticed that this graph is made up of 4 different graphs. Each graph shows determinations of national well-being such as; cellphone service cost, annual hours worked, health expenditures, and annual minimum wage, in various different countries.  US is highlighted in purple in every graph to distinguish where the nation falls within the topic of the graph. Most show that the US has a significant difference in wealth, spending, and work hours compared to other countries. For example in 2017 the health expenditures in most countries was more or less between 8-12%, while the US's health expenditures was between 16-18%.
I wonder how much these graphs would look like in the year 2020 because of how much the economies around the world changed. Cell phone services and health expenditures would have probably risen while minimum wage would have probably lowered. I also wonder if the US' health expenditures were higher than other countries in 2017 because we don't have free health care like other countries do. 
This impacts my community because knowing how much the pandemic would impact this graph, it makes me curious to see where the US would fall in correlation to other countries in 2020. These graphs appeared in an article titled "The U.S. Is Lagging Behind Many Rich Countries. These Charts Show Why. "; makes me wonder if we are still "lagging" or if most countries are in our position as well. 
A headline for this graph could be: "Where Would The US Fall On These Graphs In 2020?"

As time goes on, prices will only rise which will cause future generations to struggle more.

raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graphs show the four measures of economic and personal well-being of its citizens.  There are 42 countries on some or all of these graph.

The graphs appeared online in the article “The U.S. Is Lagging Behind Many Rich Countries These Charts Show Why. ” (URL in the release.)  By viewing the graphs online, you can see the name of the country for each point on the graphs.

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and “What impact does this topic have on you?”  Better insights result from your discussing with your classmates what you all notice and wonder.  After you’ve learned from others, then respond online.  

Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in these graphs. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included these graphs and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.
 
Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Keep noticing and wondering.  Stay tuned for the next release on Friday, Dec. 11 with moderation on Wednesday, Dec. 16.  The last graph of 2020 is about your choice for instant mastery!

raw_comment:
I notice how the US has the highest expenses for cellphone service and health expenditures. The minimum wage is also in the middle of other countries.

I wonder how expensive the US is compared to other countries in other areas such as college tuition, clothes, and taxes. Since people in America pay relatively lower taxes to people in socialists countries, could that a factor in why cellphone services and health expenditures are more expensive? 

This effects my community because right now, in the middle of a pandemic, many of my loved ones are struggling to pay their cell phone bills and especially healthcare bills. Lots of them got laid off and not having a salary for a couple of months really hurt them finically and emotionally. 

America vs The World: How Much Do We Spend?

raw_comment:
I noticed that the US falls on the more expensive side of things, but it does not pay its workers as much as other countries, but we work around the median for the number of hours per year. But, the US is around the same for counties that are also first world countries. 

I wonder if the graphs would look different this year given the pandemic and other financial difficulties. 

The impact that this has on our country is great. In the area where I live, it is a pretty high-middle class city. You could survive living in my town on minimum wage working 40 hours a week. This is a problem because people need to make more money in order to provide for themselves and put money into the economy. 

These graphs show how the US is doing economically compared to other countries. We have some of the highest costing services but we pay our workers the bare minimum. Something has to change here. 
"Why Minimum Wage Isn't Making the Cut"

raw_comment: I notice that US costs were much higher in the spending categories while being relatively average in money-making categories. The US was approximately in the middle of both the annual hours worked and annual minimum wage distributions. Looking at spending costs, however, the US was by far the highest. It’s interesting to see because cellphones and healthcare are deemed necessary in modern society, but the graphs show that US worker’s wages have not increased proportionally. In terms of health expenditures, US costs were substantially higher than every other country likely being an outlier. I wonder why the US chooses private health care companies over universal health care? As shown, Switzerland had about 5% fewer health expenditures as a share of GDP, using universal health care. The US higher healthcare costs may promote the economy but could negatively impact low-income families. What are the benefits of prioritizing economy over way of life? Why has the US not raised the minimum wage to potentially compensate for these high necessity costs? The impact this has on my community is that in the US, there is an immense amount of pressure to live an expensive lifestyle no matter economic status. We in need of employment, work for minimum wage which companies have kept low. However, companies, in turn, raise prices on necessities such as cellphone costs along with our costly privatized healthcare system. My headline is, “The American Dream Is No Longer Looking Very Dreamy."

## 1) Chart type
A set of **strip plots / dot plots** (one-dimensional scatter plots), shown as **four vertically stacked panels**.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting by topic**: four separate horizontal panels, each for a different metric.
- **No stacking**.
- Within each panel, countries are shown as dots positioned along a single horizontal quantitative axis.
- A highlighted dot color is used to emphasize the **U.S.** relative to other countries.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Cellphone service cost in 2019 | Quantitative | Position on x-axis in the first panel |
| Annual hours worked in 2018 | Quantitative | Position on x-axis in the second panel |
| Health expenditures in 2017, share of G.D.P. | Quantitative | Position on x-axis in the third panel |
| Annual minimum wage in 2018 | Quantitative | Position on x-axis in the fourth panel |
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Individual dots; text labels for selected countries |
| Panel topic / metric | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into four separate panels with titles |
| U.S. highlight status | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (purple for U.S., gray for others) |
raw_comment:
1.) What do I notice? I noticed how the U.S took first place out of two of the graphs, the cell phone service cost, and the health expenditures. The U.S. did roughly average when it came to minimum wage and annual hours worked placing them around where most countries are. Next thing I noticed was the different times these graphs were based upon, and how the U.S seemed to be an outlier in some graphs.
2) What do I wonder? One thing I wonder is whether or not the graphs would change if they were all from the same year or even this year, and see whether or not the pandemic affected these graphs. I also wonder why are we at the top of health expenditures? Shouldn't a well-leading country in the world be trying its absolute best to be lowering those costs and make it more accessible to all people especially since we are roughly average in our minimum wage.
3) How does this affect me? 
 This obviously affects me in the path I'm heading towards later on in life. Whenever I'm going to pay for my phone bill or health coverage, It's going to be way higher than it is in some countries. On top of that annual hours are low, so this can really make students, or immigrants from other countries starting a life in America extremely tough. 
4) Showing how the U.S. is seeming to lead almost negatively in some of these graphs, my title might be "Is America the best, at being the worst?!"

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?

I noticed that the U.S.A. had the highest cellphone service cost and health expenditures compared to all of the other countries displayed on the graph. Also, I noticed that the U.S.A. dropped towards the middle of the annual hours worked and the annual minimum wage displays.

2. What do you wonder?

I wonder what specifically “health expenditures” are. Also, I wonder why in the “spending” categories America is the highest. As well as America being in the middle of the pack for the “working/earning” categories.

3. What impact does this have on you and your community?

Well as an American, it’s very frustrating how these services that are very important are so expensive compared to a bunch of other countries. Yet, the minimum wage in America is only in the middle of the pack.

4. What’s going on in these graphs? Write a catchy headline that captures the graphs’ main idea.

These graphs are used to display how are services in America are too expensive and Americans aren’t being rewarded enough for the work that they put in.
Title: “Does Hard Work Really Pay Off?”

raw_comment:
I notice that the distribution of health expenditures is strongly right-skewed. The US is far out on the right tail, away from the main cluster of points between 8 and 12%. It appears to be a high outlier. In the graph of cell phone service where the US is also the highest value, it is unlikely to be an outlier since the distribution has a greater spread. Overall, the US has extremely high costs while only landing around the upper middle in terms of minimum wage and hours worked compared to other countries. 
I wonder why health expenditures in the US are so absurdly high compared to other countries. Everyone knows that the US has expensive health care, one example being the insane cost of insulin. However, it seems like not much is being done to fix this issue. I also wonder how these graphs would change if data from past years was shown.
This impacts me by reminding me that as a US citizen, I have to work harder than in other countries due to the higher costs of living. As someone who has been though quite a few medical issues in my life, it’s disheartening to see how much of my income will have to go into health care. In my community, people with chronic illnesses or other severe health concerns may be even more negatively affected.
These graphs demonstrate how despite the US being a rich, first-world country, life might not be that great for the average citizen compared with other countries. A title idea could be “Is Life In The US As Great As It Seems?”

raw_comment: One thing I noticed was that in relation to other countries, the dots which represented the U.S. were fairly scattered among the four graphs. However, the U.S. tended to fall into the upper half of the graph, regardless of which countries preceded and succeeded it. The U.S. has the highest cellphone service cost and highest health expenditures, but fall in the middle for annual hours worked and annual minimum wage. One thing I wonder is how our dot placement in these four graphs would differ if the same data was collected in 2020, due to how much the economy has changed due to COVID-19. Another thing I wonder is how the other countries that appear on the graph were chosen since only a few countries appear. One last thing I wonder is why the prices for phones, healthcare, and other services are so high when in relation to other countries, our annual income is not as high for how long and hard people are working. This data impacts my community as it shows how although the United States is viewed as a country of wealth and opportunities, that compared to other places, people can end up spending a lot more on services that they shouldn’t have to spend so much on. While it is true that overall, the U.S. is a wealthy country, residents tend to spend a lot more money on necessities than people in other countries. These graphs compare the U.S. to other countries in relation to expenditures and income. A catchy title could be “U.S. Expenditure and Revenue: How Do They Compare?”

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
The U.S. falls on the right side of the distribution in the “Cellphone service cost in 2019” graph as well as the “Health expenditures in 2017, share of G.D.P.” graph. On the other two graphs, “Annual hours worked in 2018” and Annual minimum wage in 2018”, the U.S. falls on the center of the distribution.
What do you wonder?
I wonder how different these graphs would look if they were from this year. I wonder how much the pandemic has affected these categories.
 What impact does this have on you and your community?
I think a lot of people believe that the U.S. is the most consistently wealthy country; a lot of people don’t realize we also have a massive wealth gap. The result that stood out to me the most was that the U.S. falls very far to the right of the distribution in the “Health expenditures in 2017, share of G.D.P.” graph, while the other countries fall to the left of the distribution. I would guess this is because we have one of the most expensive healthcare systems. It’s truly eye-opening to see just how much more we pay for healthcare.

raw_comment:
The United States is the country with the highest cell phone service cost and health expenditures. The annual hours worked is about 1.8 thousand hours in 2018. The annual minimum wage in 2018 is a little larger than $15 thousand, which means that with the annual hours worked being 1.8 thousand hours the annual minimum wage per hour would be about $8.33 if everyone was paid minimum wage.
I wonder if the graph depicting the annual hours world was calculated with only the amount of hours adult workers work or if it includes teenage/student workers. I also wonder why the average hours worked a day can be calculated for about 6.92 hours a day on a five day work week if business hours typically are 9 hours a day.
My town is considered one of those that are typically on the higher-end of the middle class. However, there are several lower income housing in our area. Those people typically work minimum wage of about $15 thousand yearly, families would, and do, struggle to provide for their families, especially with healthcare expenses and cell phone services costing so much in the United States. As a high schooler having to work less hours than the average annual hours, I would make very little money working on minimum wage in comparison to what I need to pay for college.
The graphs are depicting how the United States has the highest costing services, yet pays minimum wage workers less than other countries. A possible head line could be: The growing Cost of America

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
I noticed that the United States had the highest cellphone service cost in 2019 and health expenditures in 2017 compared to the other countries on the graph. I also noticed that the United States fell towards the middle of the annual hours worked in 2018 and the annual minimum wage in 2018 graphs.

2. What do you wonder?
I wonder what “health expenditures” include. Are health expenditures medically related? Or can public gyms be included in this category? I also wonder why the United States’ cellphone service cost is much higher than in other countries displayed on the graph.

3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
This impacts my community because, according to these graphs, these expenses are much higher than the minimum wage in the United States. How are Americans supposed to pay these high expenses with a low income? These graphs illustrate why lots of Americans are in debt and struggle to pay for basic necessities.

4. What’s going on in these graphs? Write a catchy headline that captures the graphs’ main idea.
These graphs compare the United States’ income and expenses to other countries, such as Russia, France, and China.
Headline: “Money Doesn’t Grow On Trees.”

raw_comment:
1. I notice that in these graphs, the United States is either towards the middle of the data or on the far right. The categories, “Cellphone service costs in 2019” and “Health Expenditures in 2017, share of G.D.P” show this. These two clearly show the United States to be the priciest country out of those surveyed. For the other categories, “Annual hours worked in 2017” and “Annual minimum wage in 2018” the United States is in the center of the distribution. 
2. I wonder how other countries rank across all of the categories. Though the graphs show reference countries for each category, it’s hard to gauge truly how the United States compares when each country only appears in one category. I wonder if the United States would look better or worse in comparison to other countries if say China, Italy, and Brazil were shown for reference in each category instead of just one.
3. I think this graph has an impact on a larger more continental scale. For everyone in America, it gives them a better understanding of how the country really compares to those around them and might help people (most likely younger) get a better sense on where they might want to live. For example, if someone is very keen on free healthcare, they might realize that the United States is probably not the best country for them to live in.

raw_comment:
1) I notice that the United States’ number of annual working hours and annual minimum wage are plotted in the middle of the two respective distributions. In addition, its cellphone service costs and health expenditures are plotted on the higher end of the two respective distributions. This means that the United States has a lower national well-being than that of other countries. 
2) I wonder why the United States is considered to be one of the wealthiest, happiest countries in the world when these graphs show that it does not have a high national well-being. Americans work more hours, are paid lower minimum wages, and pay more for health and cellphone services than the majority of other countries shown in these graphs.
3) As Americans, we constantly hear from society that our country is predominantly affluent and that most citizens are content with living in the U.S. However, this stereotype is clearly false; these graphs demonstrate that the United States’ national well-being is a lot lower than that of other countries. It is important for Americans to realize that while our country has several good aspects, it also has countless problems that need solutions.
4) These graphs show how the United States’ national well-being compares to that of other major countries using four determinants: cellphone service costs, annual hours worked, health expenditures, and annual minimum wage.

raw_comment:
Looking at the graphs I noticed that the United States charged the highest amount for cell phone services in 2019. The United States also ranked significantly higher than other countries in health expenditures in 2017. The US was an outlier on the health expenditures dot plot and was approximately 5% higher than the data point closest to it (Switzerland). I noticed that the US fell closer to the middle of the distribution for annual hours worked and annual minimum wage for 2018.  

I wonder why the United States has such a higher percentage of health expenditures compared to the other countries in 2017. How are the other countries that fell much higher on the dot plot for annual minimum wage in 2018 able to have such a high minimum wage? I also wonder what is holding the United States back from raising the minimum wage, when expenses are so high?

The impact that this has on my community is that we are paying very expensive rates for cellphone services and health expenditures compared to other countries. The United States also pays their workers roughly the average minimum wage compared to other countries. The very high expenses paired with the average minimum wage can be very tough on working people in my community. 

These graphs are comparing the United States to other countries on different measures including cell phone costs, health expenditures, annual hours worked, and annual minimum wage. A headline could be: “The Expenses of the American Dream”.

raw_comment:
I noticed that the United States spends the most money on cell-service and health care out of all the countries shown. Yet, the United States’ working hours and minimum wage are roughly average. A factor that could change the expenses on healthcare is whether or not a country has global healthcare. The United States does not have universal healthcare coverage, and they spend the most on healthcare, while a country like Switzerland has universal healthcare, and they spend significantly less on healthcare than the United States.

I wonder why it costs so much for cellphone service in the United States, and what factors play into the pricing of cell service? Is it solely because the cell service companies want to make more money, or could it be because there are more expenses when providing cell service in the United States? I also wonder why the countries shown in all the displays don’t stay consistent? Had the countries remained consistent throughout the displays, then the displays would have been more conclusive.

This data impacts me and my community because the costs for services such as cell service and healthcare are so high in the United States, and in the future, these costs will affect all of us, regardless of our economic status. 

In these graphs, it is evident that the United States spends more money on healthcare and cell services than any other country, while their minimum wage and hours worked is average.
“U.S. vs. the World: Why do we Pay so Much?”

raw_comment:
After observing each graph I noticed that the trend appears to be that the United States is either average or above average in all graphs. The graphs that showed cost all had the United States as the highest-priced nation for the specific graph. The other graphs which focused on information about jobs had the United States in the middle of the graph. Finally, I noticed that the United States is way above the average cost of health expenditures in 2017. It is so far above the average that it would have most likely been considered an outlier. 

I wonder why the United States is consistently ranked higher on the graphs than other nations? I also wonder if there is a correlation between annual minimum wage and annual hours worked. 

This topic impacts my community as I live in New Hampshire which just went through/is going through an opioid epidemic where those recovering are in desperate need of medical help. To see that health expenditures are absurdly high when compared to other rich countries is disturbing as it calls into question the necessity of the prices that Americans are being charged. Especially as the opioid epidemic had a greater effect on lower-income communities. 

The graphs compare different rich nations to each other on a number line that is numbered differently between each graph. As the graph focuses on the United States, it is highlighted to better show its location. A possible catchy headline for all four graphs could be “First World Countries V. U.S.”

raw_comment:
What do I notice? I notice that we are in the middle to right of the graphs in every category. I also notice that we are in the top of health expenditures, and cellphone service costs.  I also notice we are in the middle of hours worked and minimum wage. 

What do I wonder? I wonder why if our minimum wage is in the middle of the graph, why is healthcare so high? Also, why are our cellphone prices so high? Also, why are certain countries shown?

This impacts us because we have lower hours worked and a lower minimum wage, but our healthcare is very expensive. This is not good, because many people will not be able to afford healthcare and phones because of the prices.

These graphs are showing that even though we are in the middle of hours worked and minimum wage, we still are getting charged more than other countries. 

Headline. “America, a free country, but not a cheap one.”

raw_comment:
I notice that the US is in the top 50% in every single category on this graph. Some of these categories are positives, like minimum wage, but others are negative, such as cellphone service costs. I also noticed that the US is in the middle for some categories such as annual hours worked, and annual minimum wages. 
I wonder why there are only certain countries to be shown on this graph, 
such as Mexico and Greece. I wonder if they were incorporated to show the 
difference between the US and other countries. I also wonder why healthcare in the United States is so drastically higher than the other countries, and what measures they have been taking that we could implement here in the US.
The impact this has on the community is that we are paying a lot more than other countries around the world in categories such as health expenditures, and cellphone service cost. This does not correlate well with the lower hours worked and minimum wage to try and keep up with these high prices. 
These graphs show that even though US citizens work the same and make roughly the same as other companies, they are charged significantly more than other countries in categories such as health care and cell phone service. “As Our President Once Said: We’re Number One.”

raw_comment:
After observing the dot plots, I noticed that the United States charged the most for cell phone service in 2019. The United States also had the highest percentage of health expenditures in 2017. In 2018, the United States was located in the middle of the graph for annual hours worked. The United States had around the average amount of hours. In 2018, the United States was located in the middle of the dot plot representing annual minimum wage. They had about the average minimum wage amount. In each dot plot, the United States is either located at or above the median. It is hard to compare all of this data together due to the difference in the countries being assessed. 
I wonder why the United States charged the most for cell phone service in 2019 and had the highest percentage of health expenditures in 2017. It would be interesting to know why other countries had higher annual minimum wages and more annual hours worked. I would like to know if there are any common or uncommon jobs worked within each country.
My community and I were paying the most for cell phone service in 2019. Our country was charging everyone much more than any other country was charging their citizens. Jobs in the United States during 2018 paid their workers the average annual minimum wage amount. Workers in some countries received more money but workers in other countries received less. 
“Do I really need a phone?”

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that the U.S. ranks the highest in expenses (cell phone service cost and health expenditures), while the U.S is in the middle for annual hours worked and annual minimum wages. I also noticed that the U.S. has roughly 7% more health expenditures than the median amount on the graph and is an outlier. Lastly, on every graph the U.S is roughly on the right tail of the data.

2. I wonder how European countries make low health care work and what the U.S. is doing wrong to prevent them from lowering it?
I also wonder how the other countries' economies compare to the U.S’s because of the differences of the U.S. expenses?

3. The graphs show that the information impacts my community negatively because our cell phone and health expenses are so expensive, yet our annual minimum wage and annual hours worked are too low to maintain a comfortable lifestyle. Middle to lower class citizens struggle and are greatly affected by the high expenses in everyday life.

4. The graphs show that even though the U.S. has an average annual minimum wage compared to other countries, the U.S. expenses are so high that citizens don’t benefit and live comfortably with the income. 
“The United States: Get Ready to Spend”

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that the U.S. has the highest cell phone service cost and the highest health expenditures while, at the same time, averaging in cost of minimum wage. Even though Americans appear to work more than Europeans, it is not equal because the U.S. has yet to increase the minimum wage or solve the extreme expenses for cell service and healthcare.

2. I wonder what type of healthcare European countries have put in place and how the U.S. could learn from their set system in order to make healthcare more inclusive and affordable. 

3. The information on this graph impacts my community in the United States negatively because our cell phone services and healthcare are so expensive yet the average minimum wage isn’t enough to maintain those costs. These expenses greatly affect the middle and lower classes because if something such as an injury or accident occurs, the expenses will put them into a debt that they may be unable to outlive.

4. These graphical displays show that even while earning the global average minimum wage, living in the United States is anything but reasonable with expenses of every day living, 
A catchy title would be, “American Dream Only for Those Who Have Money.”

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that, in the third boxplot which portrays health expenditures, the US is by far the highest.  No country is even close, but the US is eventually followed by Switzerland and then the major clump of other countries.  There is an alarming trend displayed in these 4 graphs, which show that the US is the highest on spending like health, mentioned above, but also necessities in modern society like cell phone service.  This is alarming because, as shown in the other two graphs, the US is in the middle of the pack when it comes to annual hours worked and minimum wage.  
2. I wonder what society is like in other countries displayed based on their position in the graphs.  For example, in Switzerland or France, do they have more extra money to spend since their cell phone and health expenditures are low?  
3. These graphs show a clear trend that affects my community since I live in the US, which is that Americans have less money to spend outside of their necessities.  This affects my family like it affects many others - and will significantly affect my generation when we are eventually in college and beyond.  In the US, those making minimum wage find it extremely difficult to pay for necessities and have money left over, which is clearly shown by the graphs.
4. “Does America really put its money where its mouth is?”

raw_comment:
1. I notice that the United States ranks high in spending habits but average in compensation and working habits. According to the first graph, the United States had the maximum cell phone service cost in 2019. Also, the United States seems to be an upper bound outlier in the health expenditures in 2017 category. However, the United States falls in roughly the middle of the spectrum, closer to the median, when it comes to annual hours worked in 2018 and annual minimum wage in 2018. 
2. I wonder why the United States has such a high ingrained sense of consumerism since worker compensation does not seem to promote this? Why does the United States continue to rely on mainly-privatized health expenditures if it clearly puts its people at disadvantages? Finally, I wonder why different countries are labeled in each graph? Did the statistician purposefully integrate bias?
3. These graphs show that members of my community may feel pressure to sustain an expensive lifestyle from lower incomes. The graphs show that “essentials,” such as health care and cell phones, are not proportionally charged to what many workers make in a year. These patterns negatively affect me. I feel pressure to participate in high spending habits, even though I am paid below the United States' average value for minimum wage.
4. “High United States Spending Patterns Despite Average Worker Compensation”
The United States continues to dominate consumer spending habits with relatively low income levels.

raw_comment:
A) I noticed that the US is placed near or slightly above the centers of the distributions for hours worked and minimum wage. When it came to basic services, I noticed that the US was the maximum value in both distributions (costs of cell service and healthcare). I was most interested in Health Expenditures as a share of GDP. I noticed that the US pays WAY more in healthcare costs than other countries. I hear a lot of people criticizing ideas like Medicare-for-All by saying that it’s ‘too expensive.’ If that’s the case, why is it that other countries, many of which have universal healthcare, have less costly healthcare systems than the US (as a % of GDP)?
B) I wonder why some of the points in each plot are labeled and some aren’t. For example, why are Canada and Switzerland labeled in the healthcare plot? Some of the labeled points seem to be maximums or minimums of the distributions, but the ones in the middle confuse me. Some plots have three points labeled in the middle, others two.
C) Americans have to pay way more for basic services than people in other countries. I think part of that is that many other countries have better social safety nets and public services than the US. Lack of these basic services can be detrimental to many working class Americans.
D) “Ironically, the Land of the Free Is Pretty Expensive.”
In general, while American workers are paid about what one would expect and work a reasonable amount of hours, they have a much higher cost of living.

## 1) Chart type
A set of **strip plots / dot plots** (one-dimensional scatter plots), shown as **four vertically stacked panels**.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting by topic**: four separate horizontal panels, each for a different metric.
- **No stacking**.
- Within each panel, countries are shown as dots positioned along a single horizontal quantitative axis.
- A highlighted dot color is used to emphasize the **U.S.** relative to other countries.

| Annual minimum wage in 2018 | Quantitative | Position on x-axis in the fourth panel |
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Individual dots; text labels for selected countries |
| Panel topic / metric | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into four separate panels with titles |
| U.S. highlight status | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (purple for U.S., gray for others) |

- **Small multiples / faceting by topic**: four separate horizontal panels, each for a different metric.

raw_comment: I notice that America's cellphone service cost is the highest and is an apparent outlier for having an extremely high health expenditure percentage. I also noticed that America is approximately around the median for hours worked and minimum wage. I wonder what correlation these might have with one another. It seems that America demands the most money from itś citizens with high health expenditures and cellphone costs, while also having a low minimum wage. These numbers would impact my community because 35% of Tulsa lives in poverty. Although these are older numbers, inflation and the pandemic would prove to be catastrophic for those in America only making minimum wage. With many minimum wage jobs such as restaurants, construction, retail, and fast food being severely slowed in current times, it will be harder for these people to earn money. In addition, many jobs in 2020 have moved to working from home. This would cause the demand for more work hours in a day and cellphone service to increase their prices. A title could be 'Countries that Cost More than They Pay'

raw_comment:
We noticed that the United States had a median value in regards to Annual Hours Worked and Annual Minimum Wage, however fell on the high end of the graphs when comparing Cellphone Service Cost and Health Expenditures.

We wondered if the Cellphone Service Cost was really the most relevant data to include, as some more undeveloped countries might not have as much access to this and therefore might skewer the data collected. We also wondered if the type of government (such as if it was socialist or capitalist) would play a role in the costs that the citizens of the country would be paying more for.

This impacts my community, as it gives us a snap shot of the economy - both globally and domestically. It also shows us the services we can expect to pay more for and the working environment we will most likely be in (hours and wages).

"A High Price to Pay for the American Dream."
